stem: A group of medical geneticists hypothesizes that epidermal growth factor (EGF) could induce colorectal cancer (CRC) cells to undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transition, thereby enhancing their ability to invade and migrate. The group wants to study the relationship between EGF gene polymorphism and CRC. It plans to determine EGF A61G polymorphism by using PCR-restriction fragment length polymorphism method in 249 patients diagnosed with CRC and in 261 patients without a diagnosis of CRC. Which of the following is the most appropriate null hypothesis for this study?

options.B: Hazard ratio is not equal to 1
options.D: Odds ratio is not equal to 1
options.F: Relative risk is not equal to 1

explanations.A: Hazard ratio and relative risk are used in cohort studies and clinical trials, not case-control studies.
explanations.B: Hazard ratio is not equal to 1 represents an alternative hypothesis for a survival analysis.
explanations.D: Odds ratio is not equal to 1 is the alternative hypothesis (no association = 1).
explanations.E: Relative risk cannot be calculated in a case-control study.
explanations.F: Relative risk is not equal to 1 is an alternative hypothesis for a cohort study.

generalExplanation: Participants are initially selected by disease status (249 cases with CRC and 261 controls without CRC) and compared for prior exposure (EGF A61G polymorphism), making this a case-control study. The measure of association in a case-control study is the odds ratio (OR), and the null hypothesis states no association (OR = 1).
educationalObjective: The odds ratio (OR) is the measure of association in case-control studies, and its null hypothesis is always OR = 1.

stem:
A gynecologic oncology research institute isolates a potential tumor marker for endometrial cancer. A large multicenter study is then performed to evaluate serum levels of the tumor marker in women with and without endometrial cancer. The following curves are generated using the results of the study.

Clinical researchers decide to use the tumor antigen to develop a confirmatory test for patients with suspected endometrial cancer. During preliminary design of the test, the cutoff point for positive/negative results is set at point A. If the cutoff point is moved from A to B, the specificity of the test will change in which of the following ways?

explanations.A: Moving the cutoff from A to B raises the threshold, decreasing false positives and increasing specificity.
explanations.B: Moving the cutoff from A to B increases specificity (fewer false positives) while decreasing sensitivity (more false negatives).
explanations.D: Changing the cutoff point alters both sensitivity and specificity.

generalExplanation: Raising the cutoff point from A to B means fewer healthy patients without endometrial cancer will test positive (fewer false positives, more true negatives), which increases specificity (TN / [TN + FP]) at the expense of decreased sensitivity.
educationalObjective: Raising the cutoff point of a quantitative diagnostic test increases specificity (fewer false positives) and decreases sensitivity (more false negatives).

stem: A new test is devised to detect HIV. It has a sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 85% compared to the gold standard. The test is used in 2 populations: a population in Africa with a 20% prevalence of HIV, and a population in Asia with a 1% prevalence of HIV. Which of the following is the most accurate statement concerning the new test?

options.A: The negative predictive value of the test is lower in the Asian population
options.B: The positive predictive value of the test is higher in the African population
options.C: The sensitivity of the test is higher in the African population
options.D: The specificity of the test is higher in the Asian population
options.E: The test is not valid in the African population

explanations.A: NPV increases as disease prevalence decreases, so NPV is higher in the Asian population (1% prevalence).
explanations.C: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic test properties that do not vary with disease prevalence.
explanations.D: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic test properties that do not vary with disease prevalence.
explanations.E: Validity (sensitivity 90%, specificity 85%) does not change by population prevalence.

generalExplanation: Positive predictive value (PPV) increases with higher disease prevalence because true positives increase relative to false positives. Since HIV prevalence is higher in the African population (20%) than in the Asian population (1%), PPV is higher in the African population.
educationalObjective: PPV increases and NPV decreases with higher disease prevalence, whereas sensitivity and specificity remain independent of prevalence.

stem: A group of investigators plans to conduct a study to assess the relationship between colon cancer and elevated plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. The study design involves determining the prevalence of elevated plasma CRP levels (based on prespecified cutoff values) and of colon cancer in a sample of individuals at a given point in time. The prevalence of elevated CRP levels is compared between patients with and without colon cancer. Which of the following is the best statement of the null hypothesis for this study?

options.A: Colon cancer is more prevalent among subjects with elevated CRP levels
options.B: Having a diagnosis of colon cancer does not affect plasma CRP levels
options.C: Subjects with elevated plasma CRP levels are prone to colon cancer
options.D: The risk of colon cancer is the same for subjects with and without elevated plasma CRP levels
options.E: There is no association between elevated plasma CRP level and colon cancer

explanations.A: This states an alternative hypothesis (an association exists).
explanations.B: Cross-sectional studies cannot establish temporal direction (whether cancer preceded CRP elevation).
explanations.C: This states an alternative hypothesis with a causal/temporal direction.
explanations.D: This describes a cohort study null hypothesis comparing incidence/risk over time.

generalExplanation: This is a cross-sectional study measuring elevated plasma CRP and colon cancer simultaneously at a single point in time. Because temporality cannot be established, the null hypothesis should simply state that there is no association between elevated plasma CRP level and colon cancer.
educationalObjective: The null hypothesis states no relationship between exposure and outcome, and its phrasing must match the study design.

stem: A clinical research center conducted a study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a topical quick-penetrating solution (QPS) of heparin compared to heparin topical gel in the prevention of infusion-associated phlebitis. Two hundred patients undergoing intravenous cannulation for at least 72 hours were enrolled and randomized to receive 6-8 drops of QPS of heparin or 1 g of heparin sodium topical gel over the cannulated vein every 8 hours for a total of 10 doses. After 72 hours, results show that the incidence of phlebitis is 60% in the QPS group and 75% in the gel group. The reduction in incidence is statistically significant. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of these results?

explanations.C: NNT = 1 / 0.15 = 6.7 ≈ 7 (rounded up to the nearest whole number).

generalExplanation: The control group (gel) risk is 0.75 and the treatment group (QPS) risk is 0.60. Thus ARR = 0.75 − 0.60 = 0.15 (15%), RRR = 0.15 / 0.75 = 20%, and NNT = 1 / 0.15 = 6.7, which rounds up to 7 patients.
educationalObjective: Number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 / ARR, rounded up to the nearest whole number.

stem:
A case-control study is conducted to ascertain the role of ethnicity and various risk factors in predicting pregnancy-related deaths among women who identify as Black or as Non-Hispanic White. Women in both groups who experienced pregnancy-related deaths in the United States over a 7-year period are matched to healthy women with live births. Selected characteristics of the study population and findings are included below:

The overall unadjusted odds ratio for pregnancy-related deaths for Black compared with Non-Hispanic White women is 3.07 (95% confidence interval, 2.78-4.20). After controlling for socioeconomic status, maternal age, hypertension, tobacco and alcohol use during pregnancy, and receipt of obstetric prenatal care, the odds ratio for pregnancy-related deaths for Black women compared with Non-Hispanic White women is 2.65 (95% confidence interval, 2.12-3.45). Which of the following most accurately describes the adjusted odds ratio finding for pregnancy-related deaths in Black compared to Non-Hispanic White women?

options.A: Black women are more likely to experience pregnancy-related death primarily due to poverty and low receipt of obstetric prenatal care
options.B: The increased odds of pregnancy-related deaths in Black women are potentially explained by external factors not adjusted for in the study
options.C: The case-control study design is not efficient to draw statistically significant conclusions about differences in pregnancy-related deaths
options.D: The risk of pregnancy-related deaths is approximately 3 times higher among Non-Hispanic White women compared to Black women
options.E: When adjusting for contraception use, advanced maternal age likely contributes significantly to increased pregnancy-related deaths in Black women

explanations.A: Even after adjusting for poverty, prenatal care, and the other listed factors, the OR remained significantly elevated (2.65; 95% CI: 2.12–3.45).
explanations.C: Case-control studies are efficient for studying rare outcomes such as pregnancy-related death.
explanations.D: The odds were ~3 times higher among Black women compared to Non-Hispanic White women, not the reverse.
explanations.E: Maternal age >35 did not differ significantly (p = 0.12), and contraception use was not adjusted for.

generalExplanation: After adjusting for socioeconomic status, maternal age, hypertension, substance use, and prenatal care, the odds ratio decreased slightly from 3.07 to 2.65 but remained statistically significant (95% CI: 2.12–3.45). This indicates that unmeasured external factors (eg, structural discrimination) not adjusted for in the model may contribute to the remaining disparity.
educationalObjective: An association that remains statistically significant after adjusting for known confounders suggests that additional unmeasured factors contribute to the association.

stem: The parents of a neonate recently diagnosed with early-onset Pompe disease come to the office for follow-up. They state that while doing extensive research on possible treatments for the disease, they found a single scientific report about a new therapy for Pompe disease. The parents request this new therapy instead of the standard enzyme replacement therapy. The single report describes a study that included 15 neonates who received the new therapy immediately after diagnosis. The study reports that the therapy lengthened survival and improved motor development and cardiac function in infants based on a comparison with published prognostic outcomes of patients with this condition. It does not compare cases of early-onset Pompe disease to controls. Which of the following statements is the most accurate in this situation?

options.A: A case series with a larger sample size could determine treatment effectiveness
options.B: A prospective cohort study would be superior to a randomized control trial
options.C: A randomized control trial will show that the new therapy is more effective than the standard therapy
options.D: The study does not offer enough evidence to recommend the new therapy
options.E: There is no evidence of selection bias in the study

explanations.A: Observational studies (including large case series) lack randomization/control and cannot establish treatment efficacy.
explanations.B: Randomized controlled trials are the gold standard for evaluating treatment efficacy, superior to cohort studies.
explanations.C: An RCT is needed to test efficacy, and it may or may not show the new therapy is superior.
explanations.E: Subject selection methods are not described, so selection bias cannot be ruled out.

generalExplanation: A report of 15 neonates without a concurrent control group is a descriptive case series. Observational designs cannot establish causal treatment efficacy or provide sufficient evidence to recommend a new therapy over standard treatment.
educationalObjective: Descriptive observational studies (eg, case series) cannot establish causal relationships and do not provide sufficient evidence to recommend a new treatment.

stem:
An oncologic research institute isolates an antigen associated with colon cancer. A study is conducted to evaluate serum levels of the potential tumor marker in patients with suspected colon cancer who are undergoing colonoscopy at a regional gastroenterology clinic. The following curves are generated using the results of the study.

Researchers decide to use the tumor antigen to develop an adjunct test for colon cancer in high-risk patients. Assuming disease prevalence in the study group is similar to that in the target population, moving the cutoff point from B to A will change the positive predictive value in which of the following ways?

explanations.A: Because the curves are symmetric, moving from B to A increases TP and FP by the same absolute amount, which decreases PPV.
explanations.C: Lowering the cutoff increases false positives relatively more than true positives here, decreasing PPV.
explanations.D: Changing the cutoff alters TP and FP, changing PPV.

generalExplanation: Moving the cutoff from B to A lowers the threshold, increasing both true positives (TP) and false positives (FP) by the same amount x. Because PPV = TP / (TP + FP), adding x to the numerator and 2x to the denominator decreases PPV.
educationalObjective: Lowering a diagnostic cutoff when TP and FP increase equally decreases the positive predictive value (PPV).

stem:
Graduate students at a school of public health are analyzing the results of a study they conducted at a community health fair. The students approached fairgoers at random and asked them if they would be willing to answer questions about health-related topics; 90% of those approached agreed to participate. Using a prewritten questionnaire, the students asked the participants standardized questions and recorded the answers. In addition to obtaining basic demographic data, students inquired about the amount of carbonated beverages consumed in each household and also asked participants to estimate prevalence of obesity in their household. By comparing the demographic data they gathered to those from a recent official demographic census, the students determined that the fair was well attended by a representative sample of the community. Their results suggest that the self-reported prevalence of obesity among household members is approximately 25% and that there is no association between household consumption of carbonated beverages and reported prevalence of obesity.

Item 1 of 2
Which of the following best describes the study design?

explanations.A: Case-control studies select participants by disease status.
explanations.B: Ecological studies use populations rather than individuals as the unit of analysis.
explanations.C: Experimental studies assign an intervention.
explanations.E: Prospective cohort studies follow participants over time.

generalExplanation: The students conducted a cross-sectional survey assessing risk factors (carbonated beverage consumption) and outcomes (obesity) at a single point in time. Cross-sectional studies are observational studies.
educationalObjective: Cross-sectional surveys are observational studies that measure exposure and outcome at a single point in time.

stem:
Item 2 of 2
The students subsequently mail out an anonymous questionnaire to members of the same community. The questionnaire is of similar length as the one administered during the fair, and the questions are phrased similarly. The response rate and the demographics of the sample are comparable to those of the survey taken at the fair. However, when the students analyze the data from the returned anonymous questionnaires, they find that the self-reported prevalence of obesity among household members is significantly higher than that estimated at the fair, and their results suggest that households with higher carbonated beverage consumption have a higher reporter prevalence of obesity. Which of the following forms of bias is most likely responsible for these differences in results?

explanations.A: Ascertainment bias occurs when a nonrepresentative sample is selected; here demographics matched the census.
explanations.B: Berkson bias occurs when hospital-based controls are used.
explanations.C: Neyman (prevalence) bias occurs when rapidly fatal cases are missed.
explanations.D: Response rates and demographics were comparable between the two surveys.

generalExplanation: Participants interviewed face-to-face at the fair likely under-reported carbonated beverage intake and household obesity due to perceived social stigma, whereas anonymous mailed questionnaires yielded more candid responses. This is reporting bias.
educationalObjective: Reporting bias occurs when participants over- or under-report exposures or outcomes due to social desirability or perceived stigma.

stem: The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) conducted during 2017-2018 estimated that the mean amount of total sugars consumed per day by adults age ≥20 is 107 grams with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 104-110 grams. If the confidence level is increased to 99%, which of the following are the most likely lower and upper confidence limits for the 99% CI?

options.A: Lower confidence limit: 102; Upper confidence limit: 108
options.B: Lower confidence limit: 102; Upper confidence limit: 112
options.C: Lower confidence limit: 104; Upper confidence limit: 110
options.D: Lower confidence limit: 106; Upper confidence limit: 108
options.E: Lower confidence limit: 106; Upper confidence limit: 112

explanations.A: The sample mean (107) must be the midpoint of the interval, and the 99% CI must be wider than 104–110.
explanations.C: 104–110 is the 95% CI; a 99% CI must be wider.
explanations.D: 106–108 is narrower than the 95% CI.
explanations.E: 106–112 is not centered at the sample mean of 107.

generalExplanation: For the same data, increasing the confidence level from 95% to 99% always widens the confidence interval, and the sample mean (107 grams) remains the exact midpoint. Only 102–112 is centered at 107 and wider than 104–110.
educationalObjective: A confidence interval with a higher confidence level is always wider than one with a lower confidence level, and the sample estimate is always its midpoint.

stem: Consecutive readings of pulmonary capillary wedge pressure were obtained from a patient in the intensive care unit using a Swan-Ganz catheter. The readings are 20 mm Hg, 22 mm Hg, 21 mm Hg, 22 mm Hg, and 18 mm Hg. Which of the following is the median of the values given above?

explanations.A: 18 mm Hg is the minimum value.
explanations.B: 20 mm Hg is the second value when ordered.
explanations.C: 20.6 mm Hg is the arithmetic mean: (18 + 20 + 21 + 22 + 22) / 5 = 20.6.
explanations.E: 22 mm Hg is the mode (most frequent value).

generalExplanation: Ordering the 5 observations from lowest to highest gives {18, 20, 21, 22, 22}. The middle value (median) is 21 mm Hg.
educationalObjective: The median is the middle value of an ordered dataset.

stem: A resident conducts a case-control study to evaluate the association between the use of diuretics and bladder cancer. A sample of 100 patients with bladder cancer is randomly selected from the state cancer registry, and a sample of 100 patients who have been admitted for any reason other than cancer is randomly selected from the resident's hospital. The resident then evaluates medical charts to determine the frequency of past or current use of diuretics among cases and controls. The results of the study reveal that past or current use of diuretics has a significant protective effect against bladder cancer (odds ratio: 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.67-0.89). The resident's results contrast with the findings from a population-based study in which the incidence of bladder cancer is equal among those who use diuretics and those who do not (relative risk: 1.01; 95% CI: 0.92-1.25). Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the resident's study results?

explanations.A: Attrition bias arises from loss to follow-up in longitudinal studies.
explanations.B: Observer bias occurs when investigators are unblinded and misclassify data.
explanations.C: Recall bias occurs when cases and controls recall past exposures differently on questionnaires.
explanations.D: Response bias occurs when participants give socially desirable answers on surveys.

generalExplanation: Selecting hospitalized patients as controls creates Berkson bias, a type of selection bias. Hospitalized controls typically have a higher prevalence of diuretic use than the general population, artificially making diuretics appear protective against bladder cancer.
educationalObjective: Berkson bias is a type of selection bias that occurs when controls are chosen exclusively from hospitalized patients, who may have different exposure rates than the general population.

stem: The administration of a university hospital conducted a cross-sectional study of errors in the medication use process (MUP) across all hospital departments. The MUP incorporates a wide variety of scenarios, including timing errors, dosing errors, and adverse events. The results of the study showed that in a random sample of 360 patients receiving treatment in the emergency department, the prevalence of MUP errors is 32.7% (95% confidence interval: 24.3-41.4). The director of the emergency department had previously reported that the prevalence of medication errors was approximately 25%. Based on these data, which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.A: The director is incorrect because the estimated prevalence is 32.7%
options.B: The results are affected by ecological fallacy because they involve all hospital departments
options.C: The results do not contradict the director because the confidence interval includes 25%
options.D: The study cannot evaluate statistical hypotheses because it is a cross-sectional study

explanations.A: 32.7% is a point estimate; any value within the 95% CI (24.3%–41.4%) is plausible.
explanations.B: The unit of analysis is the individual patient (360 ED patients), so ecological fallacy does not apply.
explanations.D: Cross-sectional studies can be analytical and test hypotheses.

generalExplanation: A 95% confidence interval (24.3%–41.4%) represents the range of plausible values for the true population prevalence. Because 25% lies within this interval, the study results do not contradict the director's estimate.
educationalObjective: A confidence interval provides a range of plausible values for the true population parameter and can be used to evaluate claims about population values.

stem: A new test is devised to measure the serum level of a specific protein. A sample of blood is taken from a patient, and the new test is performed 3 times with results of 162, 186, and 247 IU/dL. Using the traditional reference test (considered the gold standard), the patient's serum protein level is determined to be 184 IU/dL. A measurement within 5% of the reference test value is considered accurate. Based on these results, the new test most likely has which of the following characteristics?

options.E: Precision and accuracy cannot be determined

explanations.A: The repeat measurements (162, 186, 247) vary widely (low precision), and only 1 of 3 falls within 5% of 184 (174.8–193.2).
explanations.B: Wide scatter across repeat measurements indicates low precision.
explanations.C: Only 1 of 3 measurements (186) falls within the accurate range (174.8–193.2 IU/dL), indicating low accuracy.
explanations.E: Both precision and accuracy can be evaluated from these data.

generalExplanation: Precision (reliability) reflects consistency across repeat measurements; 162, 186, and 247 IU/dL are widely scattered, indicating low precision. Accuracy (validity) reflects closeness to the gold standard (184 ± 5% = 174.8–193.2 IU/dL); only 1 of 3 measurements falls in this range, indicating low accuracy.
educationalObjective: Precision is reproducibility across repeat measurements, while accuracy is closeness to the gold-standard reference value.

stem: An otorhinolaryngology resident conducted a cross-sectional study on neurocognitive dysfunction in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS). The study hypothesis stated that the cognitive dysfunction symptoms reported by patients may be related to severity of rhinologic symptoms, facial pain, or chronic inflammation seen in CRS. A correlation analysis of pain and cognitive dysfunction, disease-specific quality of life, and clinical measures of disease severity were conducted. Initial study results showed that lower levels of cognitive dysfunction tended to relate to lower scores in pain severity and that the relationship was very weak but statistically significant. Based on this information, which of the following statements is most correct about the correlation coefficient?

options.A: It is negative and probably closer to −1 than to 0
options.B: It is negative and probably closer to 0 than to −1
options.C: It is positive and probably closer to 0 than to 1
options.D: It is positive and probably closer to 1 than to 0

explanations.A: Both variables decrease together, so the correlation is positive (r > 0).
explanations.B: Both variables decrease together, so the correlation is positive (r > 0).
explanations.D: A very weak relationship corresponds to an r value closer to 0 than to 1.

generalExplanation: Because lower levels of cognitive dysfunction relate to lower pain severity scores (both variables move in the same direction), the correlation coefficient r is positive (r > 0). Because the relationship is very weak, r is closer to 0 than to 1.
educationalObjective: The correlation coefficient r indicates direction (positive when variables move together) and strength (values closer to 0 indicate weaker relationships).

stem: A large-scale randomized, double-blinded clinical trial was conducted to evaluate the effect of beta-blocker therapy on the survival of patients with chronic heart failure, class IV. The patients with severe heart failure were randomly assigned to receive either carvedilol (a beta blocker) or a placebo. In their report of the results of the study, the investigators included a table with baseline characteristics (eg, age, race, prevalence of hypertension) of the patients in the treatment and placebo groups. According to that table, both groups had a similar distribution of these characteristics. With the information given, which of the following is most probable?

options.C: The power of the study is big
options.E: Observer bias might be an issue

explanations.A: Sample size adequacy and statistical power cannot be determined from a baseline characteristics table.
explanations.B: No outcome results are provided.
explanations.C: Sample size adequacy and statistical power cannot be determined from a baseline characteristics table.
explanations.E: Observer bias is prevented by double-blinding.

generalExplanation: Randomization aims to distribute known and unknown confounders evenly across treatment and control groups. Similar baseline characteristics between the carvedilol and placebo groups indicate that randomization was successful.
educationalObjective: In clinical trials, similar baseline characteristics between treatment and control groups indicate successful randomization.

stem:
The drug ad in the exhibit button applies to the next 2 items

The drug advertisement is focused on kalgatran (Kalaxin), a new oral anticoagulant for the treatment of non-valvular atrial fibrillation.

Item 1 of 2
Bleeding risk is the major concern when anticoagulating patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation. The advertisement promotes Kalaxin as a safe medication. In the study comparing Kalaxin and warfarin, which of the following specific bleeding risks were most similar between the 2 groups?

explanations.A: GI bleeding was significantly higher with Kalaxin (HR = 1.75; 95% CI: 1.52–1.94).
explanations.B: Intracranial bleeding was significantly lower with Kalaxin (HR = 0.39; 95% CI: 0.21–0.52).
explanations.C: Life-threatening bleeding was significantly lower with Kalaxin (HR = 0.75; 95% CI: 0.61–0.94).
explanations.E: Total bleeding was slightly lower with Kalaxin (HR = 0.91; 95% CI: 0.86–0.96).

generalExplanation: As stated in the text beneath the bar graph on page 2 of the Kalaxin drug ad, major bleeding had a hazard ratio of 0.96 (95% CI: 0.84–1.10; 2.8% vs 2.9%). Because the HR is closest to 1.0 and its 95% CI includes 1.0, major bleeding risk was most similar between the two groups.
educationalObjective: A hazard ratio close to 1.0 with a 95% confidence interval including 1.0 indicates no statistically significant difference between treatment and control groups.

stem:
Item 2 of 2
When assigning patients to treatment and control groups, proper randomization is important to avoid the effect of extraneous variables in the study results. In the current study, which of the following forms of additional information would help most in determining randomization success?

explanations.A: Annual stroke rates are a study endpoint rather than a measure of randomization success.
explanations.C: Compliance charts reflect treatment tolerability, not randomization success.
explanations.D: Follow-up rates reflect retention/attrition, not randomization success.
explanations.E: Subgroup analyses examine effect across strata rather than baseline balance.

generalExplanation: Successful randomization balances potential confounders across treatment and control groups. Comparing a table of baseline patient characteristics between the two groups confirms whether they started with similar features.
educationalObjective: Successful randomization in a clinical trial minimizes selection bias and is confirmed by comparing baseline patient characteristics between groups.

stem: Two cross-sectional studies were conducted using different questionnaires to determine the prevalence of over-the-counter analgesics use in a population. The first study showed a prevalence of 7.5% (95% confidence interval 6.0 - 9.0), and the second study demonstrated a prevalence of 7.3% (95% confidence interval 6.9 - 7.6). If the true prevalence of over-the-counter analgesics use in the population is 7.4%, which of the following statements about the results of the study is the most accurate?

options.A: The first study results are more specific
options.B: The second study results are more sensitive
options.C: The first study results are more valid
options.D: The first study results are more accurate
options.E: The second study results are more precise

explanations.A: Sensitivity and specificity of the questionnaires cannot be determined from these data.
explanations.B: Sensitivity and specificity of the questionnaires cannot be determined from these data.
explanations.C: Both studies have estimates very close to the true value (7.4%), so both appear similarly valid/accurate.
explanations.D: Both studies have estimates very close to the true value (7.4%), so both appear similarly valid/accurate.

generalExplanation: Precision reflects random error and is indicated by the width of the confidence interval. The second study has a much narrower 95% CI (6.9–7.6) than the first (6.0–9.0), making the second study more precise.
educationalObjective: Precision is a measure of random error; a narrower confidence interval indicates greater precision.

stem: A randomized, double-blind trial is conducted that evaluated the effect of benazepril plus amlodipine (intervention) compared to benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide (control) for hypertension in high-risk patients. A total of 11,203 patients with hypertension who were at high risk for cardiovascular events were randomly assigned to receive treatment with either benazepril plus amlodipine (n = 5,544) or benazepril plus hydrochlorothiazide (n = 5,659). The primary end point was the composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, hospitalization for angina, resuscitation after sudden cardiac arrest, and coronary revascularization. There were 552 primary-outcome events in the benazepril-amlodipine group and 679 in the benazepril-hydrochlorothiazide group. Difference between groups was statistically significant (p < 0.001). Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of these results?

explanations.A: 0.10 is the risk in the intervention group (552 / 5,544 ≈ 0.10); ARR = 0.12 − 0.10 = 0.02.
explanations.B: 0.83 is the relative risk (0.10 / 0.12 ≈ 0.83), not ARR.
explanations.C: 0.12 is the risk in the control group (679 / 5,659 ≈ 0.12), not RR.
explanations.E: 0.02 is the absolute risk reduction (0.12 − 0.10 = 0.02), not RRR.

generalExplanation: Risk in the control group is 679 / 5,659 ≈ 0.12, and risk in the treatment group is 552 / 5,544 ≈ 0.10. Thus RR = 0.10 / 0.12 ≈ 0.83, ARR = 0.12 − 0.10 = 0.02, and RRR = (0.12 − 0.10) / 0.12 ≈ 0.17 (or 1 − 0.83 = 0.17).
educationalObjective: Relative risk reduction (RRR) = (Risk_control − Risk_treatment) / Risk_control = 1 − RR.

stem:
A prospective, randomized controlled trial compared the rates of serious medical errors made in intensive care units (ICUs) by interns working a traditional schedule and interns working an intervention schedule. The traditional schedule was extended (≥24 hr) work shifts every other shift (an every-third-night call schedule); the intervention schedule eliminated extended work shifts and reduced the number of hours worked per week. Incidents were identified using a multidisciplinary 4-pronged approach that included direct, continuous observation. Two physicians who were unaware of the interns' schedule assignments independently rated each incident. The study involved 2,450 patient-days, 1,200 during the traditional schedule and 1,250 during the intervention schedule. It represented 634 admissions to the ICUs (385 during the traditional schedule and 249 during the intervention schedule) and 5,888 hours of direct observation of interns. An excerpt of the study results is shown below.

Which of the following is the approximate proportion of decreased risk in nonintercepted serious errors per patient-day among interns in the intervention schedule relative to those in the traditional schedule?

explanations.A: 0.02 (25 / 1,250) is the rate in the intervention schedule.
explanations.B: 0.03 (0.05 − 0.02) is the absolute risk reduction.
explanations.C: 0.05 (60 / 1,200) is the rate in the traditional schedule.

generalExplanation: The rate of nonintercepted serious errors per patient-day is 60 / 1,200 = 0.05 in the traditional schedule and 25 / 1,250 = 0.02 in the intervention schedule. The relative risk reduction (RRR) is (0.05 − 0.02) / 0.05 = 0.60.
educationalObjective: Relative risk reduction (RRR) = (Rate_control − Rate_treatment) / Rate_control = 1 − RR.

stem: A medical student conducting a literature search about breastfeeding and HIV is reviewing a randomized controlled trial in which women who were HIV seropositive were randomly assigned to either breastfeed or formula feed their infants. After delivery, mother-infant pairs were followed monthly during the first year and quarterly during the second year until the mother's death, or until 2 years after delivery. The study reported that the cumulative mortality rate at 24 months after delivery was 11.2% in the breastfeeding group and 3.5% in the formula-feeding group (p = 0.02). Based on these results, what is the approximate percentage of maternal deaths in the breastfeeding group that can be attributed to breastfeeding?

explanations.A: 3.2 (11.2% / 3.5%) is the relative risk.
explanations.B: 3.5% is the mortality rate in the formula-feeding (nonexposed) group.
explanations.C: 11.2% is the mortality rate in the breastfeeding (exposed) group.
explanations.D: 13 is the number needed to harm (1 / 0.077).

generalExplanation: Attributable risk percentage (ARP) = [(Risk_exposed − Risk_nonexposed) / Risk_exposed] × 100 = [(0.112 − 0.035) / 0.112] × 100 = 68.75% ≈ 68.8%.
educationalObjective: Attributable risk percentage (ARP) = [(Risk_exposed − Risk_nonexposed) / Risk_exposed] × 100.

stem: A group of pediatric oncologists conducts a study in which exposure to radiation from CT scans is compared between children with a diagnosis of leukemia at age <15 and children (age and sex matched) without a diagnosis of leukemia. Information is also obtained on birth weight, maternal smoking, parental socioeconomic status, and background gamma radiation. Data on CT scans are collected from medical records in 2 university hospitals. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure of association for this study?

explanations.A: Hazard ratio and median survival are used in cohort studies and clinical trials.
explanations.B: Hazard ratio and median survival are used in cohort studies and clinical trials.
explanations.D: Prevalence ratio is used in cross-sectional studies.
explanations.E: Relative risk is used in cohort studies and clinical trials, not case-control studies.

generalExplanation: Participants are selected based on outcome status (children with leukemia vs matched children without leukemia) and compared for past CT radiation exposure, making this a case-control study. The appropriate measure of association is the odds ratio.
educationalObjective: Case-control studies compare past exposure between cases and controls using the odds ratio.

stem: A group of genetic epidemiologists conducts a case-control study to explore whether the presence of estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) in breast tissue in women with benign breast diseases (BBD) is associated with subsequent development of breast cancer. Women with breast cancer and prior BBDs (860 cases) are matched to women with prior BBD who have been diagnosed as free from breast cancer (1,720 controls). The matching factors are age at BBD diagnosis, type of BBD, and follow-up time since BBD diagnosis. ER and PR expressions are obtained from the specimens of women with BBD. The study shows an association between higher expressions of ER and PR and subsequent breast cancer in women with BBDs that is statistically significant at the 1% level. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the study results?

options.A: About 1 of 100 of women with BBD who have higher ER/PR expression will develop breast cancer in their lifetime
options.B: An association between higher ER/PR expression and subsequent breast cancer development in women with BBD will occur by chance less than 1% of the time if no such association is expected
options.C: In women with BBD, at least 1% of subsequent breast cancer is due to higher ER/PR expression
options.D: Personalizing the clinical management of women with BBD and higher ER/PR expression may reduce their risk for subsequent breast cancer by 1%
options.E: Women with BBD and higher ER/PR expression have at least a 1% higher risk for subsequent breast cancer than women with BBD and lower ER/PR expression

explanations.A: The 1% significance level (alpha = 0.01) does not indicate absolute lifetime risk.
explanations.C: The 1% significance level does not measure attributable risk or causality.
explanations.D: The 1% significance level does not measure risk reduction.
explanations.E: The 1% significance level does not measure the magnitude of risk.

generalExplanation: Statistical significance at the 1% level means alpha = 0.01 and p < 0.01. The p-value represents the probability of observing the study's results (or more extreme) by chance alone assuming the null hypothesis (no association) is true.
educationalObjective: A p-value < alpha (eg, 0.01) indicates that the observed association would occur by chance less than alpha% of the time if the null hypothesis were true.

stem:
A group of scientists developed a new quantitative test to diagnose a childhood disease that is lethal if left untreated. The distribution of patients who have the disease and who are disease-free according to their values on the new test are shown below.

If the treatment for the disease is safe and inexpensive, which of the points labeled on the graph represents the best diagnostic cutoff for the disease?

explanations.A: Point A also achieves 100% sensitivity but creates many more unnecessary false positives than point B.
explanations.C: Point C maximizes overall diagnostic accuracy but misses some diseased patients (false negatives).
explanations.D: Points D and E miss many diseased patients (false negatives).
explanations.E: Points D and E miss many diseased patients (false negatives).

generalExplanation: Because the disease is lethal if untreated and the treatment is safe and inexpensive, missing a case (false negative) is catastrophic, so the test needs 100% sensitivity. Point B is the highest cutoff that still captures all diseased patients (100% sensitivity) while minimizing false positives compared with point A.
educationalObjective: For lethal diseases with safe, inexpensive treatment, the optimal cutoff maximizes sensitivity (minimizing false negatives).

stem:
A 42-year-old woman comes to the office for follow-up after knee replacement surgery. BMI is 35.8 kg/m². The patient does not engage in physical activity due to her knee problems but says she is willing to try radical changes in her eating habits if it will help her lose weight. She read an article that compared the effects of alternate-day fasting (ADF) versus daily calorie restriction (DCR) on weight loss in adults. A total of 200 obese participants were randomly assigned to either ADF or DCR. The trial involved a 12-month weight-loss phase with outcomes measured at baseline and at 12 months. The primary outcome was change in body weight, and the secondary outcomes were adherence to the dietary intervention and change in cardiometabolic risk factors. The study reported a statistically significant (p < 0.05) reduction in body weight and cardiometabolic risk indicators in both groups. The difference in change from baseline to 12 months between groups is shown below.

Adverse effects such as migraines and low energy were reported by 24% of participants in the ADF group and by 32% of participants in the DCR group (p = 0.21). The study reported that 12% of participants could not tolerate ADF and switched to DCR. Based on these data, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?

options.A: ADF because of the greater reduction in body weight
options.B: ADF because of the high incidence of adverse effects in the DCR group
options.C: DCR because most participants in the ADF group switched to DCR
options.D: DCR because of the greater reduction in cholesterol values
options.E: Either ADF or DCR because the outcomes are similar

explanations.A: The 95% CI for body weight change difference (−3.1 to 1.6) includes 0, so there is no significant difference.
explanations.B: The difference in adverse effects (24% vs 32%, p = 0.21) was not statistically significant.
explanations.C: Only 12% (not most) of ADF participants switched to DCR.
explanations.D: The 95% CIs for total, HDL, and LDL cholesterol differences all include 0.

generalExplanation: All 95% confidence intervals for differences in weight loss and cardiometabolic risk factors between ADF and DCR include the null value of 0, and adverse effect rates did not differ significantly (p = 0.21). Because outcomes are similar, either diet may be recommended.
educationalObjective: A confidence interval for a difference between two groups that includes 0 indicates no statistically significant difference.

stem:
A study was done to evaluate a new serologic screening test for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. A total of 1000 people were randomly selected from the population, screened using the new test, and screened again using the gold standard (i.e., Western blot analysis) to determine true infection state. The findings are as follows:

What is the sensitivity of this new serologic screening test?

explanations.B: 140/200 is the positive predictive value.
explanations.C: 60/820 is the false-positive rate (1 − specificity).
explanations.D: 60/200 is the false discovery rate (1 − PPV).
explanations.E: 180/1000 is the disease prevalence in the sample.

generalExplanation: Sensitivity is the proportion of subjects with the disease who test positive: TP / (TP + FN) = 140 / (140 + 40) = 140 / 180.
educationalObjective: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN).

stem: Medical students are planning a case-control study to examine the association between intrapartum antibiotic (IPA) exposure and late-onset serious bacterial infection (SBI) in full-term infants. A random sample of healthy full-term infants born via vaginal or cesarean delivery who were hospitalized for late-onset SBI at age 7-90 days will be selected from the pediatric clinic's medical records. A sample of healthy, age- and sex-matched, full-term infants who are known not to have had SBI will also be selected from the pediatric clinic. Both vaginal deliveries, which do not routinely include antibiotic prophylaxis, and cesarean deliveries, which routinely include antibiotic prophylaxis, will be included in the study. IPA exposure will be defined as any maternal antibiotic use in the 24 hours prior to delivery. Previous research has shown that risk of neonatal infection, including late-onset SBI, is increased with prematurity, history of maternally transmitted infection, cesarean delivery, and comorbidities. Which of the following sources of bias is of greatest potential concern in this study?

explanations.A: Case-control studies do not involve follow-up, so attrition bias does not apply.
explanations.C: Exposure and outcome are ascertained from medical records, minimizing misclassification.
explanations.D: Exposure is obtained from medical records rather than patient recall.
explanations.E: Cases and controls are randomly selected and matched from the same clinic.

generalExplanation: Cesarean delivery is independently associated with both IPA exposure (routine antibiotic prophylaxis) and increased risk of late-onset neonatal SBI. Including both vaginal and cesarean deliveries without controlling for mode of delivery introduces confounding bias.
educationalObjective: Confounding bias occurs when an extraneous variable (eg, cesarean delivery) is independently associated with both the exposure and the outcome.
